'''Kompaneyets equation''' refers to a non-relativistic, [[Fokker–Planck equation|Fokker–Planck type]], [[Boltzmann equation|kinetic equation]] for [[photon]] [[number density]] with which photons interact with an electron gas via [[Compton scattering]], first derived by [[Alexander Kompaneyets]] in 1949 and published in 1957 after declassification.<ref>Kompaneets, A. (1957). The establishment of thermal equilibrium between quanta and electrons. Soviet Journal of Experimental and Theoretical Physics, 4(5), 730-737.</ref><ref>Oliveira, G. E. F., Maes, C., & Meerts, K. (2021). On the derivation of the Kompaneets equation. Astroparticle Physics, 133, 102644.</ref>  The Kompaneyets equation describes how an initial photon distribution relaxes to the equilibrium [[Bose–Einstein statistics|Bose–Einstein distribution]]. Kompaneyets pointed out the radiation field on its own cannot reach the equilibrium distribution since the Maxwells equation are linear but it needs to exchange energy with the electron gas. The Kompaneyets equation has been used as a basis for analysis of the [[Sunyaev–Zeldovich effect]].<ref>Sunyaev, R. A., & Zeldovich, Y. B. (1970). Small-scale fluctuations of relic radiation. Astrophysics and Space Science, 7, 3-19.</ref>

==Mathematical description==
Consider a non-relativistic electron bath that is at an equilibrium temperature <math>T_e</math>, i.e., <math>k_B T_e\ll m_e c^2</math>, where <math>m_e</math> is the electron mass. Let there be a low-frequency radiation field that satisfies the soft-photon approximation, i.e., <math>\hbar\omega \ll m_ec^2</math> where <math>\omega</math> is the photon frequency. Then, the energy exchange in any collision between photon and electron will be small. Assuming homogeneity and isotropy and expanding the collision integral of the [[Boltzmann equation]] in terms of small energy exchange, one obtains the Kompaneyets equation.<ref>Bernstein, J., & Dodelson, S. (1990). Aspects of the Zel'dovich-Sunyaev mechanism. Physical Review D, 41(2), 354.</ref>

The Kompaneyets equation for the photon number density <math>n(\omega,t)</math> reads<ref>Zel'dovich, Y. B., & Syunyaev, R. A. (1972). Shock wave structure in the radiation spectrum during Bose condensation of photons. Soviet Journal of Experimental and Theoretical Physics, Vol. 35, p. 81, 35, 81.</ref><ref>Milonni, P. W. (2021). Simplified derivation of the Kompaneets equation. Physics of Plasmas, 28(9).</ref>

<math display="block">\frac{\partial n}{\partial t} = \frac{\sigma_Tn_e\hbar}{m_ec}\frac{1}{\omega^2}\frac{\partial}{\partial\omega}\left[\omega^4\left(\frac{k_BT_e}{\hbar}\frac{\partial n}{\partial\omega}+ n^2+n\right)\right]</math>

where <math>\sigma_T</math> is the total [[Thomson scattering|Thomson cross-section]] and <math>n_e</math> is the electron number density; <math>\lambda_e = 1/(n_e\sigma_T)</math> is the Compton range or the scattering [[mean free path]]. As evident, the equation can be written in the form of the continuity equation

<math display="block">\frac{\partial n}{\partial t} + \frac{1}{\omega^2}\frac{\partial }{\partial \omega}(\omega^2 j)=0,\quad j =  -\frac{\sigma_Tn_e\hbar}{m_ec}\omega^2\left(\frac{k_BT_e}{\hbar}\frac{\partial n}{\partial\omega}+ n^2+n\right).</math>

If we introduce the rescalings

<math display="block">\tau = \frac{\sigma_Tn_ek_B T_e}{m_e c} t, \quad x = \frac{\hbar\omega}{k_B T_e}</math>

the equation can be brought to the form

<math display="block">\frac{\partial n}{\partial \tau} = \frac{1}{x^2}\frac{\partial}{\partial x}\left[x^4\left(\frac{\partial n}{\partial x}+ n^2+n\right)\right].</math>

The Kompaneyets equation conserves the photon number

<math display="block">N= \frac{Vk_B^3T_e^3}{\pi^2c^3\hbar^3}\int_0^\infty n\,x^2dx</math>

where <math>V</math> is a sufficiently large volume, since the energy exchange between photon and electron is small. Furthermore, the equilibrium distribution of the Kompaneyets equation is the [[Bose–Einstein statistics|Bose–Einstein distribution]] for the [[photon gas]],

<math display="block">n_{\mathrm{eq}} = \frac{1}{e^{x-\mu_0}-1}</math>

where <math>\mu_0=\mu/k_BT_e.</math>
